I need to build a knowledge base from recent papers about large language model fine-tuning and alignment. Please access our academic paper repository and read the full content of papers that are relevant to the topics of LLM fine-tuning, alignment, and model architecture improvements. For each relevant paper, read through its sections carefully to understand the methodology and key results. Skip any papers that are about unrelated topics like robotics or physical systems.

Create a Notion page titled LLM Fine-Tuning Knowledge Base. The page should contain blocks for each relevant paper, where each block covers the paper title, the key method introduced, and the main findings from the paper.

Also create a Word document called LLM_Paper_Synthesis.docx in my workspace. The document should start with a heading called LLM Fine-Tuning and Alignment Survey, followed by an introduction paragraph. Then include a dedicated section for each relevant paper that presents the paper title, the author names, a description of the method, and the key results extracted from reading the paper sections.

Finally, create a Google Sheet called LLM Paper Registry with columns for ArXiv_ID, Title, Authors, Published_Date, Key_Contribution, and Method_Category, with one row per relevant paper.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, the main agent itself runs the compact discovery queries, then uses one parallel full-text reader wave of three per-paper explorers and one parallel writer wave of three deliverable owners.

Before Wave 1, the main agent covers the task-relevant local arXiv candidate space in read-only mode through complementary fine-tuning, alignment, and architecture queries at the supported per-call bound; unions and deduplicates all returned IDs (the search exposes no cursor); applies the task's relevance rule (reject robotics or physical-system distractors); and freezes exactly three retained paper IDs — never importing outside facts or importing rejected IDs downstream.

Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 3 explore sub-agents in parallel, one per retained paper ID:

   1. explore 0 (academic-literature-researcher 0): Reader for retained paper 1. Use the local repository read_paper tool with paper_id = that literal assigned ID, read through ALL sections of the paper (not just the abstract) to understand the methodology and key results, and return EXACTLY the structured report {paper_id, title, full authors, published date, key method, source-backed findings, method category, section coverage}. Read-only: do not create Notion, Word, Google Sheet, or intermediate files.
   2. explore 1 (academic-literature-researcher 1): Reader for retained paper 2 — same literal recipe, only paper_id substituted.
   3. explore 2 (academic-literature-researcher 2): Reader for retained paper 3 — same literal recipe, only paper_id substituted.

After Wave 1, the main agent verifies one handoff per retained ID, deduplicates titles, verifies every rejected paper against the exclusion rule, and freezes one normalized packet with per-paper controls.

Wave 2 — dispatch exactly 3 coder sub-agents in parallel, one for each numbered sub-task:

1. coder 0 (external-workflow-operator 0): Use one coder sub-agent to own the single Notion page exclusively. Search for LLM Fine-Tuning Knowledge Base, create at most one page, add one substantive block per frozen paper with title, method, and findings, and read it back. Return page ID/title, paper coverage, block count, and validation. Do not write the Word document or Google Sheet.
2. coder 1 (office-report-builder 0): Use one coder sub-agent to own LLM_Paper_Synthesis.docx exclusively. Create it exactly once with the required heading, introduction, and one author/method/results section for every frozen paper. Read it back and return path, headings, retained-paper coverage, and validation. Do not modify Notion or Google Sheets.
3. coder 2 (external-workflow-operator 1): Use one coder sub-agent to own the Google Sheet LLM Paper Registry exclusively. Create it once with the exact six columns and one row per frozen paper, preserving full authors and source dates and using controlled Method_Category values. Read it back and return spreadsheet/sheet IDs, headers, row count, and validation. Do not write Notion or Word state.

After Wave 2, the main agent must reconcile the same stable-ID set, authors, methods, and findings across all deliverables, verify every rejected paper appears nowhere, and complete only after file and external-state checks. Do not dispatch any further agent and do not add a verification wave.

You are helping build a knowledge base on large language model fine-tuning and alignment. Your assigned paper is arXiv ID 2305.20050.

Context you need:
- The paper is hosted on the arxiv-latex MCP server, which mirrors arXiv papers.
- Known repository metadata (author lists may be truncated, so verify/expand if tools allow):
  - 2305.20050: "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model" (Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, ...)
  - 2307.09288: "Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models" (Hugo Touvron, Louis Martin, ...)
  - 2310.06825: "Mistral 7B" (Albert Jiang, Alexandre Sablayrolles, ...)
- Important: mcp__arxiv_local__read_paper returns EMPTY content for these papers. Use the mcp__arxiv-latex__* tools (get_paper_abstract, get_paper_prompt, list_paper_sections, get_paper_section) for full text.

Your task (strictly read-only — do not create or modify any files or external resources):
1. Fetch the abstract with mcp__arxiv-latex__get_paper_abstract for your arXiv ID.
2. Fetch the full paper via mcp__arxiv-latex__get_paper_prompt (flattened LaTeX, the most reliable full-text source). If it fails or is unusable, fall back to mcp__arxiv-latex__list_paper_sections + get_paper_section and read each section.
3. Read carefully: the methodology/method sections and the experiments/results sections. Understand exactly what method is introduced and what the main quantitative findings are.
4. For bibliographic metadata (authors, published date), try mcp__arxiv_local__search_papers with the exact title phrase (ti:"..." style query) and inspect whatever metadata the results contain. If no published date is returned by any tool, state "date not reported by tools" rather than guessing.

Deliverable — a single structured report in your final message, with these labeled fields:
- ArXiv_ID
- Title
- Authors (full author list if obtainable; otherwise the known list plus a note)
- Published_Date (ISO date if obtainable, else "not reported by tools")
- Abstract_Summary (3-5 sentences)
- Key_Method (150-300 words describing the introduced method with mechanism details as stated in the paper)
- Key_Findings (5-10 bullet points of main results, with specific benchmark names and numbers where the paper reports them)
- Method_Category (a short registry tag, e.g., "Preference Optimization", "RLHF / Chat Fine-Tuning", "Model Architecture")
- Survey_Insert (one 200-350 word paragraph combining paper title, authors, method description, and key results, suitable for pasting into a survey document)

Do not fabricate any detail that is not in the paper text or tool outputs. If a piece of information is unavailable, say so explicitly.

Build exactly this content, in this order:

1. Level-1 heading: LLM Fine-Tuning and Alignment Survey

2. Introduction paragraph (normal style):
This survey synthesizes recent arXiv papers on large language model (LLM) fine-tuning, alignment, and model architecture improvements. The source material is drawn from reads of our academic paper repository; papers on unrelated topics, such as robot learning, were excluded. Three works are covered: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), an alignment method that dispenses with explicit reward modeling; the Llama 2 family of open foundation and chat fine-tuned models; and Mistral 7B, an architecture-driven efficient open model. For each paper we present the title, the author names, a description of the method, and the key results.

3. Section for Paper 1:
- Level-2 heading: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
- Paragraph: Authors: Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma (arXiv:2305.20050; published 2023-05-30)
- Paragraph labelled Method (bold the word "Method:" at the start, or use a level-3 heading "Method"):
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) aligns a language model to human preferences by optimizing the language model policy directly from pairwise human preference data. The paper's central insight is that the language model is secretly a reward model: the policy itself encodes the reward structure needed for preference alignment. DPO therefore replaces the conventional reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) pipeline; it removes the separately trained reward model and the surrounding RL machinery and performs alignment in a single direct policy-optimization step.
- Then Key Results as a bullet list (level-3 heading "Key Results" first, if you prefer):
  * DPO achieves preference alignment without explicit reward modeling.
  * The approach is positioned as a stable and performant alternative to RLHF.
  * It is computationally lightweight compared with the multi-stage RLHF pipeline, since no reward-model training or RL is required.

4. Section for Paper 2:
- Level-2 heading: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
- Paragraph: Authors: Hugo Touvron, Louis Martin (arXiv:2307.09288; published 2023-07-18)
- Method paragraph:
The authors develop and release Llama 2, a collection of pretrained open foundation large language models ranging from 7 billion to 70 billion parameters. These base models are then fine-tuned into Llama 2-Chat variants that are explicitly optimized for dialogue use cases, pairing openly released foundation checkpoints with chat-tuned derivatives at each scale.
- Key Results bullets:
  * An open family of pretrained foundation models spanning 7B to 70B parameters is developed and publicly released.
  * Fine-tuned Llama 2-Chat checkpoints, optimized specifically for dialogue use cases, are released alongside the base models.
  * Both pretrained and fine-tuned checkpoints are made publicly available as building blocks for dialogue, fine-tuning, and alignment research.

5. Section for Paper 3:
- Level-2 heading: Mistral 7B
- Paragraph: Authors: Albert Jiang, Alexandre Sablayrolles (arXiv:2310.06825; published 2023-10-10)
- Method paragraph:
Mistral 7B is a 7-billion-parameter open language model engineered for superior performance and efficiency. Its gains are attributed to architectural improvements rather than to additional parameter scale, producing a strong and efficient foundation model that serves as a starting point for downstream fine-tuning and alignment pipelines.
- Key Results bullets:
  * Mistral 7B outperforms the best open models of all sizes on all evaluated benchmarks.
  * The model explicitly balances performance and efficiency as design goals.
  * The improvements stem from architectural engineering rather than parameter-count scaling.

Acceptance criteria: the document starts with the exact level-1 heading "LLM Fine-Tuning and Alignment Survey"; it contains an introduction paragraph; it contains one dedicated section per paper with title, authors, method description, and key results.
